messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina, an 80-year-old African woman who had spent most of her life working as a midwife, described the accident as the point at which ordinary life had split into a before and after. She had been travelling in a car when it was struck in a violent collision, metal buckling around her, the cabin becoming a pinned, helpless space while noise, smoke, and the sudden, bewildering stillness of being trapped flooded over her. What stayed with her most was not only the impact itself but the sense that her body had been caught and damaged in a way she could not undo. In the weeks afterward, she began to dread enclosed places, especially any room that felt locked or difficult to leave. Even small reminders of the crash could pull her back there: the shrill approach of sirens outside her home or on the street, or the sight of a car mangled by an accident scene on television or passing in traffic, would leave her tense and braced, as if the danger were returning. Those moments were not just upsetting; they set off a wave of arousal that made it hard for her to settle. She found it difficult to fall asleep, and when she did drift off she often woke again, listening for sounds she could not name, already on guard. By day she became increasingly superalert, scanning hallways, doors, and roadways, and she startled badly at ordinary noises that would once have barely registered. Being so watchful made the remembered car crash feel close again, and the more her body stayed keyed up, the more strongly those same reminders seemed to demand her attention.

As Amina lived with these reactions, her thinking about the accident hardened into painful conclusions. She said, with a kind of quiet shame, that somebody else would not have gotten into such a situation, as if her own judgment had somehow failed her. At the same time, the pain and stiffness she felt in her body after the accident made her increasingly certain that she had been permanently damaged. She came to talk about her life in broad, defeated terms, saying that the trauma had destroyed it, and this belief made each reminder feel heavier and more consequential. When she saw a car crumpled at the roadside, or heard a siren in the neighborhood, she did not experience these as neutral cues; they seemed to confirm that the world was still dangerous and that she was not the person she had been before. Her fear of being caught again in a confined, locked place became especially strong when she had to use elevators or sit in a room with the door closed, because those moments seemed to echo the trapped feeling in the car and to prove that her body was still vulnerable. In turn, the nights when she could not sleep and remained on guard left her more raw and jumpy the next day, and in that exhausted state she noticed danger everywhere. Ordinary sounds made her jump, and the bodily jolt would send her mind straight back to the accident, making her even more convinced that her body had been permanently damaged and that her life, in its old form, was gone.

Before long, Amina began organizing her days around these fears. She avoided locked or confined spaces whenever she could, preferring open areas of her home and insisting on doors left unlatched, because being enclosed made her think of the crushed car and the helplessness of being unable to move. She steered away from routes where sirens were common and found herself turning off the radio or television when crash scenes came on, especially images of cars hit by accident. In her work and daily routine, this had concrete costs: as a midwife she had once been used to moving calmly through other people’s emergencies, but now she became hesitant about anything that might place her in a crowded or hard-to-exit environment, and she withdrew from some of the errands and visits that had once structured her week. Yet these efforts did not bring relief for long. The more she avoided the reminders, the more unfamiliar and dangerous they seemed, and when she did encounter them unexpectedly, they landed with full force because she had been trying so hard not to think about them. That made her even more certain that the accident had permanently altered her body and destroyed the life she used to know. The belief that she was damaged and that the world had become untrustworthy kept her scanning for danger, and that constant watchfulness made every siren, every sudden noise, and every closed room feel like a threat waiting to happen. By the time she sought help, Amina was exhausted by poor sleep, strained by her constant vigilance, and increasingly frightened that she would never feel safe again. What brought her in was the realization that she was no longer simply remembering the accident; she was living inside its aftermath every day, and she wanted help before fear took over the rest of her life.
